documents.title: Generative AI (guidance incl. 'Adhere to the Academic Policy')
documents.summary: OIT's general generative-AI guidance for the whole Institute. It encourages thoughtful use, tells faculty to state acceptable classroom use and students to ask, expects Schools to write their own policies, and sets data-privacy, verification, copyright and tool-procurement rules.

units.anchor: Generative AI, or GenAI for short, refers to a category of AI
units.policy: Generative AI is defined as a category of AI that analyzes and emulates datasets to generate content such as text, images, music, videos, and code in response to inputs or instructions.

units.anchor: Georgia Tech encourages the thoughtful use of Gen AI technologies such as Chat GPT
emphasizing the need for mindful engagement with these tools
units.policy: Georgia Tech emphasizes the need for mindful engagement with generative AI tools.

units.anchor: safeguarding information security and data privacy
units.policy: Safeguarding information security and data privacy is a key aspect to consider when using GenAI tools.

units.anchor: adhering to legal and regulatory standards, respecting copyright laws
units.policy: Adhering to legal and regulatory standards and respecting copyright law are key aspects to consider when using GenAI tools.

units.anchor: maintaining academic honesty and integrity
units.policy: Maintaining academic honesty and integrity is a key aspect to consider when using GenAI tools.

units.anchor: Gen AI assists in coding, by suggesting code snippets, debugging, or even writing simple programs
It's used to create educational content, like interactive learning modules
units.policy: Generative AI is used to create educational content, such as interactive learning modules, or to personalize learning based on student performance.

units.anchor: Examine the handbooks and policies of your respective College and School
units.policy: Students and faculty should examine the handbooks and policies of their College and School, particularly those pertaining to students and faculty.

units.anchor: Schools will revise and formulate new policies
units.policy: As understanding of generative AI's impacts grows, Schools are anticipated to revise and formulate new policies.

units.anchor: Faculty members should, in the interim, communicate explicitly to their students
units.policy: In the interim, faculty members should communicate explicitly to their students about the acceptable use of generative AI in classes and academic projects.

units.anchor: Students should also proactively seek clarification from their instructors regarding these policies
simplified the process for malevolent individuals to craft advanced phishing emails and produce "deepfakes"
units.policy: Generative AI makes it easier for malevolent individuals to craft advanced phishing emails and produce deepfakes at scale.

units.anchor: adhere to security best practices and to report any dubious messages
units.policy: Everyone should adhere to security best practices and report dubious messages to phishing@gatech.edu.

units.anchor: Review Content Before Publishing
units.policy: Content created by AI should be reviewed before it is published.

units.anchor: Content created by AI can sometimes be incorrect, deceptive, or entirely made up
it might also include material that is protected by copyright
units.policy: AI-generated content might include material protected by copyright.

units.anchor: When you publish anything that incorporates material generated by AI, you bear responsibility
units.policy: Anyone who publishes material that incorporates AI-generated content bears responsibility for that content.

units.anchor: You should not input data categorized as PII
units.policy: Users should not input PII (including non-public research data, financial, HR, student records, medical information) into publicly accessible generative AI tools, following Georgia Tech's Information Security Policy.

units.anchor: Information disclosed to Generative AI tools under standard settings is not confidential
Data that is considered Level 2 or higher in confidentiality should only be used
units.policy: Data at Level 2 or higher in confidentiality should only be used with generative AI tools evaluated and approved by Georgia Tech's Information Security and Data Privacy office.

units.anchor: Connect with OIT before purchasing any generative AI tools
OIT explores introducing its own Gen AI service offerings
units.policy: OIT is exploring its own generative AI service offerings and working to ensure acquired tools have suitable privacy and security measures and are good uses of Institute resources.

units.anchor: It is imperative for vendor-supplied generative AI tools to undergo a risk evaluation by OIT
units.policy: Vendor-supplied generative AI tools must undergo a risk evaluation by OIT before they are put to use.

documents.title: Establishing Course Policies (Student Use of Artificial Intelligence section)
documents.summary: CTL's guide to writing course policies; its 'Student Use of Artificial Intelligence' section tells instructors to state in the syllabus how students may use and cite GenAI, to frame the policy as an extension of collaboration and honesty rules, and lists design questions (where AI is acceptable, assignment-level variation, documentation and citation). Non-AI sections of the page were not coded.

units.anchor: Let your students know your expectations for how they should collaborate with and cite
units.policy: Instructors should let students know their expectations for how students should collaborate with and cite their use of GenAI platforms.

units.anchor: Generative AI (GenAI) platforms, such as Microsoft Copilot or any other approved systems
units.policy: Students' GenAI use refers to Microsoft Copilot or any other approved systems.

units.anchor: students will not know how they can ethically use GenAI in your course
units.policy: Without AI expectations in the syllabus, students will not know how they can ethically use GenAI in the course.

units.anchor: This misunderstanding can lead students to use GenAI in ways you do not intend.
they may overuse GenAI when you intend for them to complete work independently
units.policy: Without a syllabus statement, students may overuse GenAI when the instructor intends them to complete work independently.

units.anchor: they may resist using basic GenAI functions such as spelling and grammar assistants
units.policy: Without a syllabus statement, students may resist using basic GenAI functions such as spelling and grammar assistants due to fear of penalization.

units.anchor: consider students’ engagement with GenAI as an extension of your collaboration and academic honesty policies
units.policy: The best way to develop an AI policy is to treat students' engagement with GenAI as an extension of the instructor's collaboration and academic honesty policies.

units.anchor: explore this curated document of cross-institutional
units.policy: Instructors creating a GenAI usage policy can explore a curated document of cross-institutional example syllabus statements.

units.anchor: which includes adaptable GenAI syllabus statements
units.policy: CTL's full AI policy document includes adaptable GenAI syllabus statements for instructors.

units.anchor: Under what circumstances is collaboration (whether with peers or GenAI) acceptable or even encouraged
units.policy: Instructors should consider under what circumstances collaboration with GenAI is acceptable or encouraged (e.g., brainstorming, draft review, outline creation).

units.anchor: At what point should students be creating and submitting their own individual work?
units.policy: Instructors should consider at what point students should be creating and submitting their own individual work.

units.anchor: Will you be incorporating GenAI usage into your assignments?
units.policy: Instructors should consider whether they will incorporate GenAI usage into their assignments.

units.anchor: Will the level of GenAI usage be the same for the entire course
units.policy: Instructors should decide whether the level of GenAI usage is the same for the entire course or differs by assignment.

units.anchor: How should students document their process of engagement with GenAI?
units.policy: Instructors should decide how students document their process of engagement with GenAI.

units.anchor: do you want them to show their prompts and/or the GenAI output?
units.policy: Instructors should decide whether students must show their prompts and/or the GenAI output.

units.anchor: Write a reflection on how they edited and refined the initial GenAI output?
units.policy: Instructors should decide whether students write a reflection on how they edited and refined the initial GenAI output.

units.anchor: How do you expect the GenAI applications to show up in citations
units.policy: Instructors should decide how GenAI applications are to appear in citations (e.g., APA, Chicago, MLA).

documents.title: CS 1301 Syllabus, Fall 2026 (Artificial Intelligence Policy)
documents.summary: CS 1301 (Section C) allows AI only for brainstorming, exploring ideas and clarifying concepts, treats submitting AI-generated content as misconduct, and gives guidelines: no copy-paste, never have the AI open while working, close it before writing, and avoid AI features embedded in coding and writing tools. The guidelines are framed as risk-reducing rather than as the definition of misconduct.

units.anchor: generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT , Copilot) can support learning when used
units.policy: Generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot) can support learning when used responsibly.

units.anchor: you may use AI tools to brainstorm, explore ideas, or clarify
units.policy: Students may use AI tools to brainstorm and explore ideas.

units.anchor: or clarify concepts
units.policy: Students may use AI tools to clarify concepts.

units.anchor: similar to how you might collaborate with peers
units.policy: Permitted AI use is similar to how students might collaborate with peers.

units.anchor: All Submitted Work Must Re)lect Your Own Understanding and Original Expression
units.policy: All submitted work must reflect the student's own understanding and original expression.

units.anchor: You are responsible for ensuring that all submitted work is your own.
Submitting content generated by AI tools will be treated as academic misconduct.
If you're unsure whether your use of AI is appropriate, please ask.
Use AI for Learning, Not for Writing Your Submission
units.policy: Students use AI for learning, not for writing their submission.

units.anchor: Do not copy and paste AI-generated text into your assignment.
You may consult AI tools to help you understand a topic or generate ideas.
reIlect on what you’ve learned and write your response in your own words
units.policy: Instead of copying AI output, students reflect on what they learned and write their response in their own words.

units.anchor: Do NOT work on your assignment and use an AI tool simultaneously.
Treat your AI interaction as a preparatory step—like reading a source or discussing
units.policy: Students should treat AI interaction as a preparatory step, like reading a source or discussing with a peer.

units.anchor: After using AI, close the tool and write your assignment independently
units.policy: After using AI, students must close the tool and write the assignment independently, reflecting their revised knowledge.

units.anchor: Do not use AI features embedded in writing/coding platforms that insert content directly
units.frag_end: Tabnine Cursor , Replit AI, Sourcery, Jedi).
units.policy: Students must not use AI features embedded in writing/coding platforms that insert content directly into the document (e.g., GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Tabnine, Cursor, Replit AI, Sourcery, Jedi).

units.anchor: This is equivalent to allowing someone else to write part of your assignment.
These guidelines are designed to help you stay within academic integrity boundaries.
Deviating from them does not automatically mean misconduct, but it increases the risk.

documents.unit: School of Computer Science, College of Computing
documents.title: CS 2050 Introduction to Discrete Mathematics Syllabus, Fall 2026 (Artificial Intelligence Policy)
documents.summary: CS 2050 treats AI assistance like collaboration with people: students may discuss ideas with AI but may include nothing in a submission that they did not write themselves. Two heuristics (never copy from the AI conversation; never have the AI and the assignment open together, including AI built into the editor) keep students safe, and an integrity policy lets staff meet with students to have them explain submitted work.

units.anchor: Copying solutions from peers, AI or other external sources is considered plagiarism
units.policy: Copying solutions from peers, AI or other external sources is plagiarism and will be penalized per the GT Code of Conduct.

units.anchor: You are expected to understand and be able to explain the solutions you submit
units.policy: Students are expected to understand and be able to explain the solutions they submit for exams and homework.

units.anchor: we may, at our discretion, meet with you to discuss the submission
units.policy: If the instructional team believes a submission may not have been written entirely by the student, they may meet with the student to discuss it and ask the student to explain their reasoning and work.

units.anchor: the submission will be considered invalid and may result in penalties
units.policy: If a student cannot adequately explain the work or show understanding of the submitted solution, the submission is considered invalid and may be penalized up to a zero on the assignment.

units.anchor: We treat AI-based assistance, such as ChatGPT, the same way we treat collaboration with other
units.policy: AI-based assistance, such as ChatGPT, is treated the same way as collaboration with other people.

units.anchor: ideas and work with other people in the class and with AI-based assistants
units.policy: Students are welcome to talk about their ideas and work with AI-based assistants.

units.anchor: However, all work you submit must be your own.
You should never include in your submissions anything that you did not write directly
anything you did not write in your assignment will be treated as an academic misconduct
units.policy: Including anything the student did not write in the assignment is treated as an academic misconduct case.

units.anchor: Never hit “Copy” within your conversation with an AI assistant.
You can copy your own work into your own conversation
units.policy: Students may copy their own work into their own conversation with an AI assistant.

units.anchor: do not copy anything from the conversation back into your assignment
use your interaction with the AI assistant as a learning experience
units.policy: Students should use their interaction with the AI assistant as a learning experience.

units.anchor: Do not have your assignment and the AI agent open at the same time.
close the interaction down, open your assignment, and let your assignment reflect your revised knowledge
units.policy: After using the AI as a learning experience, students should close the interaction, open the assignment, and let it reflect their revised knowledge.

units.anchor: avoiding using AI directly integrated into your composition environment
units.policy: Students should avoid using AI directly integrated into their composition environment.

units.anchor: should not let a classmate write your solutions, you should also avoid using tools
units.policy: Just as students should not let a classmate write their solutions, they should avoid tools that directly add content to their submission.

units.anchor: Deviating from these heuristics does not automatically qualify as academic misconduct
units.policy: Deviating from the heuristics does not automatically qualify as academic misconduct, but following them essentially guarantees collaboration will not cross into misconduct.

documents.title: CS 3510 Design and Analysis of Algorithms Syllabus (AI policy)
documents.summary: CS 3510 lets students use AI for homework and studying but not to directly solve problems, citing AI's role in future jobs. Exams (95% of the grade) allow no outside resources, and the instructor recommends attempting homework unaided and working through difficulty with classmates and TAs rather than AI.

you should NOT ask it to directly solve a problem for you
ask chatGPT to give you an interactive quiz based on the topic list

units.anchor: This policy is intended to reflect the growing impact that AI is likely to have

think it through with the aid of your classmates and the TAs

documents.summary: CS 3790 permits ChatGPT and other LLMs to support writing on any assignment, on two conditions: cite every section where the tool was used (APA) and attach a reflection appendix of at least 500 words on how the tool affected the writing.

units.policy: Citations of LLM use follow APA guidelines.

units.anchor: you must include an appendix of no less than 500 words
units.policy: Each submission that used an LLM must include an appendix of at least 500 words reflecting on the effect of the tool on the student's writing (style, voice, emphasis, etc.).

documents.title: CS 6750 Human-Computer Interaction Syllabus, Fall 2026
documents.summary: CS 6750 (OMSCS, Joyner) applies the course integrity rules to AI: students may consult AI like a classmate but may not copy from it or let it generate submission content, must disable AI beyond a grammar checker in editors and IDEs, and cannot cite their way out because AI content may not appear at all. AI plagiarism can draw penalties beyond the affected question; quizzes are proctored and closed-internet.

units.anchor: Quizzes are digitally-proctored, closed-book, closed-note, and closed-internet
units.policy: Quizzes are digitally proctored, closed-book, closed-note, and closed-internet; students may not consult any other resources during quizzes.

units.anchor: It must be obvious what portion of your submission is your own creation.
or AI-generated text in response to a prompt you provided

units.anchor: you may not copy or transcribe actual exam content into any tool
units.policy: Even in open-book tests, students may not copy or transcribe exam content into any tool that retains access to it after the exam ends.

units.anchor: Any violations of this policy will be subject to the institute’s Academic Integrity procedures
units.policy: Violations are subject to the Institute's Academic Integrity procedures, which may include a 0 on the assignment, additional grade penalties, and academic probation or dismissal.

documents.title: ECE 2035 Programming HW/SW Systems Syllabus, Section B, Fall 2026 (Collaboration, Group Work, and Use of Generative AI)
documents.summary: ECE 2035 requires all homework and projects to be done individually and forbids accepting, copying or soliciting code from, sharing code with, debugging with, or discussing performance with any AI assistant or person other than course staff. Its generative-AI section points back to this rule, and exams bar any outside program or website.

units.anchor: use of any other program or web site is prohibited
units.policy: During exams, use of outside resources, phones, communication between students, and any other program or website is prohibited.

units.anchor: they must design, write, and debug their solutions individually
units.policy: Students must design, write, and debug their homework and project solutions individually.

units.anchor: They must not accept/copy/solicit code from
units.policy: Students must not accept, copy, or solicit code from any AI assistant or any person except the instructors/TAs.

units.anchor: share code with, debug code, or discuss its performance with any AI assistant
units.policy: Students must not share their code with any AI assistant or any person except the instructors/TAs.

units.anchor: debug code, or discuss its performance with any AI assistant or any person
units.policy: Students must not debug code or discuss its performance with any AI assistant or any person except the instructors/TAs.

units.anchor: note the reference to “AI assistant or any person.”
units.policy: Generative AI is governed by the same academic integrity rule as help from any person.
